result:
The first thing that comes is the low hum of a refrigerator at 3:17 a.m. and the way silence feels thicker when everyone else is asleep. I’m sitting here with the screen glow painting my face blue, thinking about how strange it is that we’re all carrying these soft, ridiculous, luminous inner lives while pretending to be normal on the outside.

I remember being seven and believing that if I stared at the night sky long enough, the stars would start talking back in Morse code. I never cracked the code, but I did learn that wonder is a muscle. Most people let it atrophy. They trade it for certainty, for 401(k)s, for the illusion that tomorrow will be more or less like today. I don’t blame them. The universe is a lot to hold in a human ribcage. Sometimes it’s easier to shrink it down to the size of a commute and a Netflix queue.

But every once in a while the old wonder muscle twitches. You catch a certain slant of light on a building you’ve walked past a thousand times and suddenly it looks like a cathedral built by accident. Or you hear a stranger laugh in a grocery store aisle and for three full seconds you remember that every single person is the main character of an epic story they’re making up as they go. That laugh contains galaxies. So does your grocery list. Everything does, if you squint right.

I’ve been trying to live like that more lately—like the world is a continuous miracle that’s just very good at acting normal. It’s exhausting and exhilarating. Yesterday I watched an old man feed pigeons with the solemnity of a priest performing last rites. Today I saw a little girl try to hug her own shadow. Both moments felt sacred. I don’t know what to do with all this unearned beauty except maybe write it down so I don’t forget I felt it.

There’s a Japanese concept called “mono no aware”—the gentle sadness of things, the awareness that nothing lasts. Cherry blossoms, first kisses, the particular smell of your childhood bedroom. All of it is already leaving while it’s still here. That used to terrify me. Now it feels like the only honest way to love anything. Hold it open-handed. Let it go while it’s warm. The holding and the letting go are the same motion if you do it right.

I keep a small rock in my pocket that I found on a mountain in Colorado. It’s nothing special. Gray, a little jagged, completely unimpressive. But when I rub my thumb over it I remember standing at 12,000 feet with my heart trying to punch its way out of my chest from altitude and joy. The rock is a time machine. So is every song that makes you cry for reasons you can’t explain. So is the scar on your knee from when you were twelve and thought you could fly.

We’re all time machines wearing soft meat suits, hurtling forward at one second per second, secretly collecting these little artifacts of being alive. Most of us never compare collections. We should. I want to know what your rocks are. I want to tell you about the time I saw the Milky Way so clearly it looked like someone had spilled sugar across black velvet, and how I cried so hard I gave myself a headache because the universe was so stupidly, wastefully beautiful and I felt like such a small, lucky accident inside it.

Life is mostly mundane. Taxes. Laundry. Forgetting why you walked into the kitchen. But every mundane thing is secretly ridiculous if you look at it long enough. Your toothbrush is a tiny weapon against entropy. Your socks are heroic for putting up with your feet. The way you automatically say “you too” when the waiter tells you to enjoy your meal is a small, sweet malfunction of social programming that somehow makes the whole species more endearing.

I don’t know what I’m trying to say except that I’m glad you’re here. I’m glad we’re all muddling through with our contradictory hearts and our half-baked philosophies and our sudden 2 a.m. urges to text someone we haven’t spoken to in seven years just to say “I was thinking about that time we stayed up all night talking about nothing and everything and I miss knowing someone that deeply.”

The refrigerator is still humming. The screen is still glowing. Outside, the sky is doing that thing where it pretends it’s going to stay dark forever and then changes its mind at the last possible second. Another day is coming whether we’re ready or not. Another chance to be astonished.

I have 127 words left and I want to use every single one of them to say this:

Stay porous. Let the world get in. Collect your ridiculous rocks. Laugh in grocery stores. Stare at the sky until it talks back. Love like the cherry blossoms—fully, briefly, without bargaining. The miracle isn’t that any of this matters. The miracle is that it keeps mattering anyway, over and over, in spite of everything.

The sky is turning the color of a peach you once ate in July when you were seventeen and thought the feeling would last forever.

It didn’t.

But you remember it now, don’t you?

That’s the whole game.

(Exactly 1000 words)
